title: The Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem

items.title: The logarithmic derivative of a meromorphic function
Zero and pole counts weighted by multiplicity and winding number
The logarithmic derivative has residue equal to local order
items.strategy: Factor a holomorphic zero as (z-a)^m h(z) with h(a) nonzero, and write a pole by the reciprocal form. Differentiating the logarithm of the factorization isolates the simple principal part m/(z-a) or -m/(z-a).

items.title: The argument principle for an admissible null-homologous cycle
items.strategy: The logarithmic derivative is meromorphic with simple residues given by local orders at the zeros and poles. Summing those residues over the finitely many singularities inside the cycle and applying the residue theorem gives the weighted count formula.

items.title: The argument-principle integral is the winding number of the image cycle
items.strategy: Compose the cycle with f and use the contour-change identity for the logarithmic derivative to rewrite the integral as the normalized argument increment of the image curve. The winding-number formula from the global Cauchy page then identifies the result.

items.title: The argument principle counts preimages of a target value
items.strategy: Apply the argument principle to f-w. Its zeros are exactly the preimages of w, with the same local multiplicities, and its poles are the poles of f.

items.title: The weighted argument principle
items.strategy: Multiply the logarithmic derivative by a holomorphic test function g. The only singularities are still the zeros and poles of f, and each residue is scaled by the value of g at that point, so the residue theorem yields the displayed weighted sum.

items.title: Rouche's theorem in the classical strict-inequality form
items.strategy: Join g to f by the nonvanishing boundary homotopy g+t(f-g). The image winding number about 0 is constant along the homotopy, so the argument principle gives the same interior zero count for the endpoints.

items.title: Rouche gives the standard leading-term proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra
items.strategy: On a sufficiently large circle, the lower-degree tail of a polynomial is strictly smaller than its leading term. Rouche then gives the degree count and the remark records the agreement with the library's canonical fundamental-theorem page.

items.title: Small perturbations preserve the total local zero multiplicity
items.strategy: Choose a small disc containing exactly the chosen zero cluster and no boundary zero of the reference function. Rouche on the boundary transfers the total multiplicity inside the disc to every sufficiently small perturbation.

items.title: Locally uniform convergence preserves the total multiplicity near an isolated zero
items.strategy: Use the Weierstrass convergence theorem to place the approximating functions uniformly close on a small boundary circle around the isolated zero. The local Rouche corollary then fixes the interior zero count for all sufficiently late functions.

items.title: Hurwitz's zero-free limit theorem
items.strategy: If the nonzero limit had a zero, the continuity-of-zeros theorem would force nearby zeros of the approximating zero-free functions. Therefore a locally uniform limit of zero-free holomorphic functions is either zero-free or identically zero.

items.title: A locally uniform limit of injective holomorphic functions is injective or constant
items.strategy: Assume the limit is nonconstant and takes the same value at two distinct points. On disjoint discs around those points, Hurwitz applied to f_n-w forces two equal-value preimages for large n, contradicting injectivity of f_n.

items.title: The argument principle recovers the open mapping theorem
items.strategy: If f is nonconstant and w is near f(a), the argument principle applied on a small boundary circle around a gives a preimage count that stays positive. The remark records that this reproduces the earlier open-mapping theorem without changing the reading order.

items.title: Argument-principle multiplicity agrees with the earlier local degree
items.strategy: Compare the zero count of f-w on a small disc with the local multiplicity count already extracted from the holomorphic normal form. Both procedures count the same local sheets and therefore define the same integer.

items.title: A contour formula for a locally single-valued holomorphic inverse
items.strategy: Apply the weighted argument principle with g(z)=z to f(z)-w on a cycle that encloses exactly one simple preimage and no boundary preimage. The weighted zero sum then returns the enclosed inverse value.

title: The Argument Principle and Rouché's Theorem — Examples

items.title: The polynomial z^5 + 3z + 1 has one zero in the unit disc
items.strategy: Compare z^5+3z+1 with 3z on the unit circle. The linear term dominates there, so Rouche gives the single interior zero count.

items.title: The same polynomial has four zeros in the annulus 1 < |z| < 2
items.strategy: Count zeros in |z|<2 by comparing with z^5, subtract the unit-disc count, and interpret the difference as the number of zeros in the annulus.

items.title: The equation e^z = 3z has exactly one solution in the unit disc
items.strategy: Apply Rouche to e^z-3z and -3z on the unit circle, using the elementary bound |e^z| < 3 when |z|=1. The dominating linear term forces exactly one interior zero.

items.title: A cubic image curve winds three times around the origin
items.strategy: Evaluate the argument-principle integral for a cubic on a circle containing all three zeros. The integral equals the total zero count and therefore the winding number of the image curve about 0.

items.title: Hurwitz preserves a simple zero under local uniform convergence
items.strategy: Use the sequence f_n(z)=z+z^2/n converging to z and isolate the zero at 0 on a small disc. The continuity-of-zeros theorem shows that each large n contributes one zero there.

items.title: The inverse contour formula recovers a local inverse value
items.strategy: Apply the contour formula to f(z)=z+z^2 on a small circle around 0 and evaluate at a nearby target value w. The integral returns the unique nearby preimage branch.

items.title: The sequence z/n shows why the injective-limit theorem needs the constant escape clause
items.strategy: Each map z/n is injective, but the locally uniform limit is the constant 0. This shows that injectivity alone does not survive the limit without the stated exception.

items.title: The function e^(1/z) shows that essential singularities lie outside the argument principle
items.strategy: Inside a small circle around 0 the function has an essential singularity and infinitely many zeros of e^(1/z)-1, so there is no finite zero-minus-pole count to match the argument-principle formula.

items.title: The weak inequality |f-g| <= |g| does not suffice in Rouche
items.strategy: Take g(z)=z and f(z)=z+1 on the unit circle. Equality holds at one boundary point, but the boundary zero obstructs the usual zero-count conclusion.

items.title: FALSE: a locally uniform limit of injective holomorphic functions is always injective
items.strategy: The sequence z/n converges to a constant map, so the theorem must say injective or constant. The false statement omits exactly the required escape clause.

items.title: FALSE: the argument principle ignores multiplicity
items.strategy: Apply the formula to f(z)=z^m on a small circle. The integral returns m, so multiplicity is built into the statement and cannot be dropped.

title: Domains of Holomorphy, Plurisubharmonicity and Pseudoconvexity

items.title: Holomorphic hulls and holomorphic convexity
Basic properties of the holomorphic hull
items.strategy: Check directly from the defining inequality that K sits inside its hull, that the hull is closed, and that taking the hull twice does not enlarge it. Coordinate projections show boundedness when the set is compact.

items.title: The equal-radius polydisc boundary function
Cauchy estimates propagate from a compact set to its hull
items.strategy: Fix a polydisc radius valid over the compact set, apply the several-variable Cauchy estimates there, and then view each derivative as a holomorphic function bounded on the hull by its bound on the original compact set.

items.title: Cartan-Thullen boundary-radius theorem
items.strategy: If a hull point were closer to the boundary than the original compact set, a polydisc centered there would leave the domain while the Cauchy estimates from the smaller radius neighborhood of K would still force holomorphic extension across that boundary point. That contradicts the domain-of-holomorphy hypothesis.

items.title: Cartan-Thullen theorem
items.strategy: The boundary-radius theorem gives the domain-of-holomorphy to holomorphic-convexity direction once compact hulls are known to stay away from the boundary. For the converse, use the standard compact exhaustion and diagonal separation argument that manufactures a function blowing up along any chosen boundary approach.

items.title: A compact convex set and an exterior point admit a complex-linear separator
items.strategy: Apply strict separation in the underlying real Euclidean space and then rewrite the resulting real-linear functional as the real part of a complex-linear functional on C^n.

items.title: Convex domains are holomorphically convex
items.strategy: Separate an exterior point from the convex hull of K by a complex-linear functional and exponentiate that separator. The resulting holomorphic function is larger at the exterior point than on K, so the point cannot lie in the holomorphic hull.

items.title: Convex domains are domains of holomorphy
items.strategy: Combine convexity of the domain with holomorphic convexity of compact hulls, then apply Cartan-Thullen.

items.title: Plurisubharmonic functions
Affine reparametrization does not change the line-test definition
items.strategy: Compose the candidate function with a nonconstant affine map of one complex variable. The subharmonic line condition is preserved because such reparametrizations are holomorphic and locally biholomorphic away from degenerate cases.

items.title: The Levi form and strict plurisubharmonicity
The C^2 Levi criterion for plurisubharmonicity
items.strategy: Restrict a C^2 function to each affine complex line and compare its one-variable Laplacian with the Hermitian form built from the complex Hessian. The plane C^2 criterion for subharmonicity then becomes exactly semipositivity of the Levi form.

items.title: Decreasing limits of plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Apply the line test pointwise to the decreasing sequence. On each complex line, the limit is subharmonic or identically minus infinity by the one-variable decreasing-limit theorem.

items.title: Holomorphic pullbacks of C^2 plurisubharmonic functions are plurisubharmonic
items.strategy: Approximate the target plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth plurisubharmonic functions on slightly smaller neighborhoods, pull each approximation back by the holomorphic map using the chain rule and the C^2 Levi criterion, and then pass to the limit with the decreasing-limit theorem.

items.title: Basic stability operations for plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Check the line test after applying a nonnegative sum, a finite maximum, or a convex increasing scalar function. Each operation reduces to the corresponding one-variable closure property for subharmonic functions.

items.title: Upper envelopes of locally upper-bounded plurisubharmonic families
items.strategy: Take the upper-semicontinuous regularization of the pointwise supremum and test on each affine complex line. The one-variable upper-envelope theorem then supplies subharmonicity line by line.

items.title: Maximum principle for plurisubharmonic functions
items.strategy: Restrict to every affine complex line through a finite local maximum point. Each restriction is a one-variable subharmonic function with a local maximum, so it is constant near the center; this makes the original function locally constant, and connectedness propagates that constancy across the whole component.

items.title: The logarithm of the modulus of a holomorphic function is plurisubharmonic
items.strategy: Restrict to any affine complex line. The restriction becomes the one-variable function log|f|, which is subharmonic, so the line test gives plurisubharmonicity with the standard minus-infinity convention on the zero set.

items.title: Plurisubharmonic exhaustions and Hartogs pseudoconvexity
Hartogs pseudoconvexity yields a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion
items.strategy: Use the boundary-distance function to build a continuous exhaustion in one direction, and in the other direction combine the exhaustion with standard convex blow-up functions so that the domain carries the same plurisubharmonic boundary barrier data.

items.title: Levi pseudoconvex domains
Levi pseudoconvexity does not depend on the defining function
items.strategy: Replace a defining function rho by h rho with h positive. On complex tangent vectors the extra first-derivative terms vanish on the boundary, so the Levi form is scaled by h and keeps the same sign.

items.title: Continuous families of analytic discs
Continuity principle for domains of holomorphy
items.strategy: Assume a first analytic disc in the family leaves the domain while the boundary curves stay in one compact subset. A small Hartogs figure built from the first escaping disc would then force holomorphic extension past the domain, contradicting the domain-of-holomorphy hypothesis.

items.title: Domains of holomorphy are Hartogs pseudoconvex
items.strategy: Use the continuity principle to rule out analytic-disc families that would violate plurisubharmonicity of the negative logarithmic boundary-radius function. Hartogs figures then convert that disc-control statement into Hartogs pseudoconvexity.

items.title: Hartogs pseudoconvexity implies Levi pseudoconvexity for C^2 domains
items.strategy: One direction differentiates the boundary-distance model and applies the C^2 Levi criterion. The converse builds a local plurisubharmonic defining model from the boundary Levi condition and compares it with the negative logarithmic boundary-distance function.

title: Domains of Holomorphy, Plurisubharmonicity and Pseudoconvexity — Examples

items.title: The bidisc is holomorphically convex
items.strategy: The bidisc is a convex domain, so the convex-domain theorem already gives holomorphic convexity. This example records the conclusion in the standard model domain.

items.title: The unit ball is Levi pseudoconvex
items.strategy: Take the defining function |z|^2-1 and compute its Levi form. The complex Hessian is the identity Hermitian form, so the tangential Levi form is nonnegative everywhere on the boundary.

items.title: A convex domain is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Apply the convex-domain corollary to a concrete half-space or ball. The example exists to make the geometric route tangible before the later nonconvex counterexamples.

items.title: The holomorphic hull of a circle in C is the filled disc
items.strategy: Identify the hull of the unit circle inside C by the maximum principle: a holomorphic function on the disc is bounded on the interior by its boundary supremum. Hence every interior point lies in the hull and no exterior point does.

items.title: The holomorphic hull of a product torus in the bidisc is the closed polydisc it bounds
items.strategy: Apply the one-variable maximum principle in each coordinate and use the product structure of the distinguished boundary. The torus forces bounds on every coordinate disc and therefore on the whole polydisc.

items.title: Minus log boundary distance is plurisubharmonic on a half-space
items.strategy: For a half-space the equal-radius boundary-distance function is an affine multiple of the real part of one coordinate, so its negative logarithm is a convex increasing function of a harmonic coordinate and hence plurisubharmonic.

items.title: The bidisc minus the origin is not holomorphically convex
items.strategy: A small product torus around the origin has hull reaching the missing point, and every holomorphic function extends across that puncture by Hartogs. This one domain witnesses failure of domain of holomorphy and of holomorphic convexity.

items.title: A domain of holomorphy need not be convex
items.strategy: Take the hypersurface complement U = C^2 \ {z_1 z_2 = 1}. The function 1/(z_1 z_2-1) is holomorphic on U and singular along the removed hypersurface, while the midpoint of (2,0) and (0,2) lies on the missing set, so U is not convex.

items.title: FALSE: every domain in C^n is a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: The punctured bidisc in dimension two is the standard counterexample: Hartogs extension fills in the missing point. This records the several-variable failure point while the one-variable contrast has been rescoped to the later Weierstrass and Mittag-Leffler supplier pages.

items.title: FALSE: the union of two domains of holomorphy is always a domain of holomorphy
items.strategy: Two overlapping domains can fill in a Hartogs-type obstruction even when each piece separately carries nonextendable holomorphic functions. The statement is therefore too optimistic without extra hypotheses.
